title: Health Informatics Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For health informatics specialists broadly, the task of designing, developing, and evaluating informatics solutions is shifting toward the integration of AI-driven platforms for hospital operations [3]. With the introduction of centralized health tech ecosystem initiatives like the CMS Medicare app library, the mechanism for implementing health information technology is moving from fragmented, bespoke data exchange setups toward managing vetted digital health app distributions to improve data portability [8]. In organizations deploying patient-facing chatbots to maintain control over health information, the task of evaluating human-technology interactions now requires validating the clinical safety and accuracy of these interfaces [4][5]. For a subset of workers in organizations implementing generative AI, the task of translating nursing practice information between nurses and engineers involves the specific refinement of model prompts to align with clinical workflows [1]. In regions where state governments are regulating chatbot usage, the task of developing policies for patient information security may be altered by new requirements for algorithmic safety audits [2]. Because AI-enabled cyberattacks increase systemic vulnerability, the task of developing practices to ensure the security of patient information now requires the inclusion of AI-specific risk assessment criteria [7]. The task of troubleshooting telehealth technology applications in homes is unlikely to change because it depends on physical hardware configuration and site-specific environmental constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may shift toward managing centralized data interoperability ecosystems and validating the clinical safety and security of AI-driven operational tools.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For health informatics specialists broadly, if the trajectory toward centralized digital health distribution holds, the task of implementing informatics solutions may evolve from custom system integration to the curation and governance of interoperable app libraries [8]. Extrapolating from current regulatory trends, the task of developing strategies for modifying information technology could shift toward a continuous cycle of auditing algorithmic outputs to satisfy state-level safety mandates [2]. In organizations using advanced AI categories, the task of analyzing computer technologies to determine applicability to nursing practice may focus on optimizing data architectures for AI scalability [6]. The task of providing consultation to nurses regarding hardware configuration is likely to persist unchanged because the physical infrastructure of medical devices remains fragmented and requires localized, hands-on support [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may transition toward the governance of clinical AI ecosystems, balancing operational efficiency with state-mandated safety compliance.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For health informatics specialists in high-automation settings, the role's evolution depends on whether algorithmic certification replaces the need for human-led policy modification. In one scenario, the role further specializes into a regulatory auditing function focused on the certification of autonomous nursing systems. In a competing scenario, the task of translating nursing practice information between clinical staff and designers may be automated by high-fidelity translation models, reducing the distinct need for this intermediary role. It remains unknown if automated compliance monitors can replace human professional judgment in the development of security policies. The task of disseminating information about nursing informatics science to the profession is likely to resist change, as professional ethical frameworks are defined through human peer discourse [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a specialized regulatory role focused on the certification and auditing of autonomous clinical systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may lose its distinct identity as automated translation tools reduce the need for human intermediaries between clinical practice and system design.*

title: Information Security Analysts
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For information security analysts broadly, because non-human identities created by AI agents introduce systemic visibility deficits [103] and critical security gaps [26], the task of regulating access to safeguard information now requires the active discovery and management of orphaned non-human identities [86][93]. Because high-capability models such as Claude Mythos [15] and GPT-5.4-Cyber [85] enable the autonomous discovery of software vulnerabilities at scale [109], the zero-day timeline is collapsing [30], which shifts the task of performing risk assessments from periodic audits to continuous, real-time vulnerability awareness [22][114] and a shift toward the Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) for prioritization [116]. Because AI-assisted supply chain attacks target open-source repositories [9] and distribute malicious packages across npm, PyPI, and Go [33], the task of monitoring current reports of computer viruses now incorporates the provenance auditing of third-party software dependencies [2][94]. Because prompt injection now serves as a viable vector for remote code execution within AI-integrated environments [102][111], the task of performing risk assessments must incorporate the auditing of LLM-invoked native functions [98]. Training users and promoting security awareness is unlikely to change yet because industrialized social engineering [10] and AI-boosted voice phishing [95] continue to exploit human cognitive biases regardless of technical defenses [115].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, analysts broadly may transition toward behavioral detection and provenance auditing, while those in agentic AI environments integrate specialized governance for non-human identities and prompt-injection risk assessment.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For information security analysts broadly, if the collapse of the zero-day timeline [30] and the rise of agentic attack speeds [22] persist, the task of performing risk assessments may shift focus from mean time to detection toward closing the "post-alert gap" via automated remediation workflows [60][105]. For analysts in organizations using automated reasoning frameworks, the task of documenting computer security and emergency measures policies may transition from manual audit logs to using formal verification to produce mathematically proven compliance results [72][79]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying autonomous agents, because agent intent is an insufficient security proxy [36], the task of modifying computer security files may pivot toward the real-time governance of agent permissions using specialized governance toolkits [31][37]. Extrapolating from current quantum computing warnings [82], the mechanism for encrypting data transmissions will likely shift toward the deployment of post-quantum cryptographic standards to maintain confidentiality [43]. Reviewing violations of computer security procedures and discussing them with violators persists as a human-centric task because correcting behavioral errors requires qualitative social judgment and interpersonal negotiation [10].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, analysts broadly may move toward auditing automated remediation speed and post-quantum encryption, while the core of policy enforcement in agentic environments shifts toward real-time permission governance.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For information security analysts broadly, the scope of the occupation remains constrained by the necessity of human accountability in high-stakes security breaches. If high-capability AI models continue to automate both the discovery and patching of vulnerabilities [15][85], a primary uncertainty remains whether defensive AI creates a stable equilibrium or a recursive escalation of attack and defense speeds [14][21]. Because systemic dependencies on core software infrastructure persist, the task of coordinating implementation of computer system plans with vendors will remain a human-led activity to manage legal and organizational liability. It remains unknown whether the proliferation of "ghost breaches" mediated by AI narratives [84] will render traditional forensic evidence obsolete.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a high-level audit role focused on the verification of autonomous security systems and the management of systemic liability.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may fracture into highly specialized roles, where the majority of routine monitoring is fully autonomous, leaving humans to manage only the most complex, non-linear adversarial conflicts.*

title: Computer and Information Research Scientists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, the emergence of architectures that reduce energy consumption by 100x [18] may alter how they apply theoretical expertise and innovation to create or apply new technology. Because agentic AI benchmarks are identified as insufficient or broken [6][31], the task of evaluating work in light of established standards shifts toward the determination of minimum rater sufficiency [9] and the use of performance-prediction frameworks [15]. For a subset of workers specializing in systems architecture, the deployment of gigawatt-scale datacenters [4], innovations in tensor, context, and expert parallelism [12], and optimized GPU communications [33] change the mechanisms used to design computers and the software that runs them. For researchers focusing on safety and alignment, the requirement to protect users from harmful manipulation [7] and evaluate behavioral dispositions [8] to prevent model deception [3] alters how they conduct logical analyses of technical problems. For researchers specializing in embodied AI, the development of visually grounded interactive planning [10][11], world models [36], and enhanced embodied reasoning [32] changes how they participate in multidisciplinary projects. In resource-constrained settings, as reported in India [22], the application of theoretical expertise shifts toward the development of frugal models to maintain capability under compute constraints [14]. For a subset of scientists in the commercial AI sector, the movement toward contract-based labor models [39] may alter how they assign or schedule tasks to meet work priorities. Tasks involving the approval, preparation, and adjustment of operational budgets are unlikely to change, as these remain governed by institutional financial constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, researchers broadly will pivot toward energy-efficient architectures and new evaluation standards, while specialized subsegments move toward extreme-scale infrastructure, grounded robotic reasoning, and adversarial safety alignment.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, if current trajectories in decentralized training [19] and on-the-job learning architectures [26] hold, the reduction in iterative experimentation costs could shift how they analyze problems to develop solutions involving computer hardware and software. Extrapolating from current research into first-principles reasoning for synthetic datasets [35][44], the process of applying theoretical expertise may move toward the design of systems capable of autonomous architectural refinement. For a subset of workers specializing in quantum computing, the establishment of logical qubit standards [17] and the use of quantum-boosted AI for predicting chaos [41][42] may stabilize the mechanisms used to design computers. The task of consulting with users, management, vendors, and technicians to determine computing needs will persist unchanged because system requirements are fundamentally tied to human organizational objectives [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward the design of self-optimizing architectures and synthetic-data-driven research, reducing manual theoretical iteration while increasing the focus on high-level system constraints.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer and information research scientists broadly, the trajectory of the occupation depends on whether the field converges on centralized extreme-scale compute or decentralized frugal architectures. One outcome involves the continued scaling of gigawatt-scale infrastructure [4], which would concentrate the task of designing computers and software within a small number of hyper-scale entities. A rival outcome involves the proliferation of decentralized training [19] and frugal models [14][22], shifting the center of theoretical innovation to diverse, localized research hubs. It remains unknown whether automatic textbook formalization [5] will eventually displace the need for humans to conduct logical analyses of technical problems. The fundamental requirement to apply theoretical expertise to overcome new physical or mathematical limits resists change even at this horizon, as computational progress eventually encounters hard hardware or algorithmic boundaries [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate into a small class of extreme-scale system architects and a broad class of localized, frugal-model specialists.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the integration of autonomous architectural refinement and formalization may reduce the occupation to a high-level supervisory role focused on goal-setting and ethical constraint definition.*

title: Computer User Support Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For computer user support specialists broadly, the integration of AI agents into IT service management platforms [3] and the increase in impersonation attacks via enterprise collaboration tools [4] alter the protocols for user interaction. Because AI agents are being deployed to manage ticket intake and triage [3], the task of answering user inquiries regarding computer software or hardware operation is partially shifted to automated systems. Simultaneously, the use of fake authentication pages [2] and the impersonation of helpdesk staff via platforms like Microsoft Teams [4] force a change in how specialists investigate and resolve problems, shifting the process from trust-based verification to rigid identity-verification playbooks. This increases the importance of maintaining records of daily data communication transactions and remedial actions [O*NET 8] to provide audit trails during security breaches [1]. Physical tasks, such as setting up equipment for employee use [O*NET 2], are unlikely to change due to the requirement for manual cable installation and physical hardware placement.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation will shift toward a hybrid model where AI agents manage routine triage and human specialists focus on high-stakes identity verification and complex troubleshooting.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For computer user support specialists broadly, if the trajectory of AI-driven helpdesk governance continues [3], the task of investigating and resolving problems may move toward a zero-trust operational model. In this scenario, the specialist's role in granting access or resetting credentials is constrained by automated cryptographic verification, which reduces human discretion in identity adjudication. This shift may alter how specialists develop training materials and procedures for users [O*NET 11], prioritizing secure identity hygiene over basic software navigation. The need to confer with staff and management to establish requirements for new systems [O*NET 6] persists because organizational workflows and internal political constraints remain too idiosyncratic for algorithmic standardization.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, symbolic support tasks may be largely governed by AI agents, leaving human specialists to manage the exceptions and failures of these automated systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For computer user support specialists broadly, the trajectory of the occupation may diverge based on the evolution of AI-driven social engineering. In one outcome, symbolic support for software and account access is fully automated, leaving human specialists to focus almost exclusively on performing minor repairs to hardware [O*NET 5] and peripheral equipment. In a competing outcome, a verified human support tier may emerge for high-security environments where automated identity adjudication is viewed as a vulnerability to advanced synthetic impersonation [4]. It remains unknown whether AI can reliably distinguish between biological human social engineering and synthetic impersonation without excessive false positives. The requirement to inspect equipment and read order sheets to prepare for delivery to users [O*NET 12] resists change due to the physical variability of hardware shipments.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may split into a hardware-centric technician role as symbolic support is fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, human specialists may be retained as a mandatory security layer for high-value identity authentication to counter synthetic social engineering.*

title: Computer Network Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For network architects broadly, the shift in data center utility from general processing to "AI token factories" is altering how they develop conceptual, logical, or physical network designs to prioritize the minimization of latency and cost per token [5]. In regions affected by geopolitical instability, such as Asia and the Gulf, architects are adjusting their approach to developing disaster recovery plans to account for physical strikes on concentrated infrastructure [3][4]. For a subsegment of workers designing hyper-scale AI training clusters, the requirement for multi-gigawatt power envelopes alters the process of determining specific network hardware or software requirements, shifting focus toward proprietary high-speed fabrics and AI-specific interconnects [1][2]. In these high-density environments, adjusting network sizes to meet volume or capacity demands is now constrained by thermal boundaries and energy distribution limits [1][5]. Coordinating the installation of new equipment in these settings requires direct alignment with power infrastructure capable of supporting gigawatt-scale loads [1][2]. Standard local area network designs for administrative office use are unlikely to change significantly because they do not face these extreme power-density or geopolitical concentration pressures [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, network architects will increasingly optimize designs for token-generation efficiency, while a specialized subsegment shifts toward power-constrained interconnect design for massive compute clusters.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For network architects broadly, if current trajectories hold, the process of developing disaster recovery plans may shift from localized redundancy toward systemic regional decoupling to ensure resilience against large-scale infrastructure strikes [3][4]. For the subsegment of hyper-scale infrastructure architects, extrapolating from the emergence of multi-gigawatt sites suggests that physical network design may be increasingly dictated by thermal management and energy distribution limits rather than traditional data throughput alone [1][2]. This could lead to a tighter integration between network architecture and power systems engineering to maintain cluster coherence at scale [1][5]. Core routing protocols for general internet traffic and standard enterprise WANs will likely persist unchanged due to the massive installed base of legacy hardware and global standardization [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may bifurcate between specialists in geopolitically resilient distributed networks and those managing the integrated power-data fabrics of gigawatt-scale compute sites.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For network architects broadly, the tension between the efficiency of centralized gigawatt clusters and the security of geographic diversification remains a primary structural uncertainty [1][3]. It remains unknown whether the field will develop mechanisms for virtual coherence across high-latency distances or if physical site size will reach a hard ceiling due to power and risk constraints [1][2]. One plausible outcome involves the persistence of the gigawatt-site model as the dominant paradigm for large-scale training, accepting higher concentration risk for the benefit of lower latency [1][5]. A rival outcome suggests a forced transition to decentralized, resilient fabrics that prioritize geopolitical survival over raw training speed [3][4]. Basic network-related documentation and troubleshooting procedures for low-complexity, non-AI systems will likely resist change as they rely on stable, low-performance logic [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, network architecture remains centered on increasingly massive, single-site gigawatt clusters, with design focused almost exclusively on extreme-density interconnects.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, network architecture shifts toward highly decentralized, geopolitically fragmented fabrics that sacrifice peak performance for systemic resilience.*

title: Telecommunications Engineering Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of workers in the oil and gas sector, specialists in regions managing rapid 5G consumer expansion, and Chinese telecommunications organizations operating in the United States, operational focuses are diverging based on localized regulatory and industrial drivers [1][2][3]. In the oil and gas subsegment, the transition of private 5G from a discretionary tool to a business-critical utility alters the process of assessing existing facilities' needs [4] by prioritizing safety-critical connectivity over basic access [1]. This shift requires a more rigorous approach to estimating costs for system implementation [4] using total cost of ownership (TCO) models that incorporate workforce safety and operational reliability [1]. In regions experiencing massive consumer scale-up, the need to review and evaluate requests for system modifications [4] increases to manage network capacity as user bases scale [2]. This volume of growth increases the frequency of coordinating installation of new hardware [4] to maintain signal density across diverse geographies [2]. For Chinese telecommunications organizations facing regulatory crackdowns in the US, the role shifts toward implementing system renovation projects [4] specifically for the purpose of migrating or decommissioning data center infrastructure and network assets [3]. Inspecting sites to determine physical configuration [4] remains unlikely to change because physical conduit pathways and tower placements are constrained by existing urban and industrial footprints.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, specialists in these specific subsegments and regions will treat 5G infrastructure as a core utility or a regulatory liability, requiring higher reliability standards or managed decommissioning.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments and organizations, if current trajectories hold, the increased reliance on 5G for safety and mass-scale connectivity may lead to more stringent requirements for developing telecommunications disaster recovery plans [4] [1][2]. Because the network serves as a strategic backbone in industrial settings, the implementation of backup or recovery procedures [4] must evolve to support near-zero latency for safety-critical data [1]. In high-growth consumer regions, the requirement to monitor and analyze system performance [4] may shift toward the management of automated, AI-driven traffic steering to handle billion-user loads [2]. For organizations undergoing regulatory-driven exits, the focus may shift to documenting procedures for hardware and software installation and use [4] as part of permanent asset handover or site closures [3]. However, the need to consult with users, administrators, and engineers to identify technical requirements [4] will persist, as business and safety protocols remain grounded in human-defined operational constraints.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role for these subsets will shift toward ensuring the disaster resilience and automated performance of high-density networks or the structured decommissioning of regulated assets.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For specialists in these specific industrial, regional, and organizational contexts, the long-term trajectory remains uncertain regarding whether 5G will be superseded by satellite-native integrated networks or 6G standards. One plausible outcome is that the role shifts toward the orchestration of virtualized network functions, reducing the time spent providing user support for diagnosing network and device problems [4]. A rival outcome is that the role becomes centered on extreme hardware specialization, where supervising maintenance of telecommunications equipment [4] dominates the workload due to the physical degradation of ruggedized hardware in harsh industrial environments [1]. The requirement to document technical specifications and operating standards [4] will likely resist change, as the high error cost in mission-critical sectors necessitates permanent, human-auditable records for regulatory compliance. It remains unknown if regulatory barriers between global telecom powers will permanently fragment the technical standards these specialists must implement.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, these specialists may transition into network orchestrators focusing on the health of virtualized, autonomous systems.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may converge on high-intensity physical maintenance of ruggedized infrastructure in industrial settings.*

title: Database Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For database administrators broadly, the adoption of predictive storage tools and natural language interfaces may alter several core technical tasks. AI-driven provisioning may reduce the manual effort required to identify, evaluate and recommend hardware or software technologies to achieve desired database performance by mitigating "fear-driven over-provisioning" [1]. Simultaneously, the introduction of text-to-SQL interfaces may streamline the process to write and code logical and physical database descriptions, allowing practitioners to generate complex queries via natural language [3]. This shifts the primary labor from manual syntax construction toward the validation of AI-generated outputs [3]. However, the task to plan, coordinate, and implement security measures to safeguard information is unlikely to change, as security configurations remain dependent on specific organizational risk tolerances and legal mandates [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, database administrators may shift a portion of their technical workload from manual capacity forecasting and query writing to the oversight and validation of predictive and generative tools.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For database administrators broadly, if current trajectories in natural language querying and predictive provisioning hold, the task of selecting and entering codes to monitor database performance could move toward an auditing role [1], [3]. Practitioners may spend less time on routine hardware recommendation and more time validating the efficiency of AI-generated queries to prevent performance degradation during peak loads [3]. The necessity to test programs or databases and correct errors persists, as these tasks often involve resolving structural logical conflicts and data corruption issues that predictive tools cannot autonomously resolve [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may evolve from active manual provisioning and coding to the auditing and performance-tuning of automated database management systems.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For database administrators broadly, the long-term trajectory suggests two rival outcomes based on the evolution of database architecture. In one scenario, the complete abstraction of the storage and query layers via AI could render the task of recommending hardware technologies obsolete, shifting the occupation toward high-level data governance and the development of standards for software acquisition [1], [3]. In a competing scenario, the increasing complexity of hyper-scale, distributed environments may create a niche for specialists who manually override AI to manage extreme performance edge-cases [1]. It remains unknown whether future database management systems will fully decouple logical data modeling from physical resource allocation. The requirement to train users and answer questions is likely to resist change, as this remains tied to human organizational hierarchies and communication needs [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may transition into a governance-focused role as routine performance and query tasks become fully automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may bifurcate, with a small class of high-specialization engineers managing the physical and logical constraints that AI cannot optimize.*

title: Database Architects
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of database architects operating in AI-integrated environments, including industrial and healthcare settings, the requirement to move AI from pilot phases to production now depends on the robustness of the underlying data architecture [4]. To support hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), these architects may alter how they develop data models for applications by integrating vector stores with traditional indices to enable semantic search [1]. The process of developing database architectural strategies may shift to prioritize governed data access for autonomous AI agents over traditional human-facing interfaces [2]. In industrial contexts, architects may focus on developing methods for integrating different products to unify fragmented operational data for real-time visibility [3]. However, the task of creating and enforcing database development standards for primary systems of record is unlikely to change, as the high error cost of data corruption in core financial or legal databases precludes the use of probabilistic storage [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, a subset of database architects will prioritize the design of hybrid architectures and governed access layers to transition AI agents and industrial intelligence from experimental pilots to operational production.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subset of workers in AI-integrated or industrial environments, if the adoption of agentic data access continues, the process of writing and coding logical and physical database descriptions may become partially automated through assistants that map natural language requests to schema elements [1][2]. Extrapolating from hybrid RAG trajectories, the focus of refining system performance and functionality may shift toward managing the synchronization between embedding models and source data to prevent semantic drift [1]. This may reduce the manual effort required for documenting database schemas as orchestration layers manage the relationship between raw data and its semantic representation [2]. Despite these changes, the task of identifying and evaluating industry trends to advise management will persist, as the selection of infrastructure involves strategic trade-offs and cost constraints that remain human-led.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, database design for this subsegment may shift toward automated schema mapping and the management of semantic synchronization, reducing the burden of manual documentation.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the subset of architects managing AI-retrieval and industrial data systems, the long-term trajectory suggests a tension between autonomous optimization and regulatory requirements. If AI agents can dynamically execute the task of developing database architectural strategies based on real-time usage patterns, the human role in defining static physical descriptions may diminish [3]. Conversely, a rival outcome exists where new data provenance laws make the requirement to document and communicate database schemas more rigorous to ensure the auditability of AI-generated outputs. It remains unknown whether vector-based retrieval will eventually subsume all traditional indexing or if a permanent hybrid state will persist. The fundamental need to test databases and correct errors will resist change because the cost of systemic data failure remains catastrophic.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, database architecture for this subsegment may move toward a dynamic model where schemas are autonomously optimized by AI based on real-time usage patterns.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward high-rigor auditing and documentation of schemas to satisfy legal provenance requirements for AI systems.*

title: Data Warehousing Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, the transition toward integrated data fabrics to support real-time predictive systems may alter the development of data warehouse process models [1] and the design of warehouse database structures [5] [4]. AI-driven tools for storage optimization may reduce manual over-provisioning by predicting usage patterns [1], which could change how specialists balance optimization of data access with resource utilization factors [9]. For a subset of workers in industrial environments, the requirement to unify fragmented operational data into optimized foundations [2] may shift how they develop data extraction procedures [4]. For a subset of workers in organizations deploying AI agents, the need to remove data access bottlenecks may alter the implementation of metadata processes and frameworks [12] to ensure data is governable for autonomous consumption [3]. Mapping data between source systems and warehouses [3] is unlikely to change in this period because it requires deep semantic understanding of legacy business logic that current predictive tools do not address.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, data warehousing specialists may shift toward implementing data fabrics and AI-driven storage optimization, while a subset may specialize in optimizing metadata and access pathways for AI agents.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, if trajectories in data fabric adoption [4] and predictive storage [1] hold, the focus of resource management may shift from manual tuning to the governance of autonomous scaling policies. Specialists could spend less time on the technical configuration of storage volumes and more on defining the operational constraints under which AI manages those volumes. For those supporting AI agents, the role may shift toward the continuous governance of agent-ready data pipelines to maintain the precision required for autonomous consumption [3]. In industrial contexts, the task of implementing business rules via stored procedures or middleware [16] may be increasingly driven by the requirements of real-time visibility foundations [2]. The task of verifying the structure, accuracy, or quality of warehouse data [2] is likely to persist as a core human responsibility due to the high error costs associated with corporate financial and regulatory reporting.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition from manual resource tuning toward the governance of automated storage orchestration and the maintenance of specialized data environments optimized for AI agents.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For data warehousing specialists broadly, the long-term trajectory suggests two rival outcomes regarding the nature of the warehouse. In one scenario, the convergence of predictive resource management [1], industrial unification [2], and agent-centric access [3][4] could lead to the emergence of "liquid" data architectures where static database structures are replaced by AI-managed ephemeral environments. In a competing scenario, strict regulatory requirements for data provenance and auditability could freeze the reliance on manually defined, transparent warehouse structures to ensure legal compliance. It remains unknown whether future compute-storage separation technologies will render the concept of "warehousing" as a distinct architectural pattern obsolete. The necessity of maintaining standards for nomenclature and organization [6] will likely resist change, as shared definitions remain the fundamental requirement for cross-organizational data utility.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into the governance of AI-managed ephemeral data environments that dynamically assemble based on real-time agent requirements.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may reinforce its focus on static, transparent, and manually audited structures to satisfy stringent regulatory provenance mandates.*

title: Network and Computer Systems Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For network and computer systems administrators broadly in organizations adopting autonomous operations tools, the deployment of AI-driven IT operations may shift the task to maintain and administer computer networks from manual configuration to the oversight of autonomous detection and remediation [10]. Because AI-driven storage analytics optimize resource allocation, the task to analyze network and server resource consumption may move toward the reduction of data over-provisioning [5]. For administrators managing AI-integrated environments, the task to perform data backups and disaster recovery operations now includes executing state-rollbacks to mitigate rogue AI agent actions [9]. For a subset of workers using cloud-native or enterprise Linux environments, the use of frontier agents may automate routine security testing and cloud operations [1][2]. In enterprise mobile settings, the task to configure, monitor, and maintain email applications involves implementing end-to-end encryption for mobile devices [7]. In high-performance data center settings, the adoption of hardware optimizations shifts the task to monitor network performance toward managing denser resource concentrations [3]. For those maintaining containerized or unpatched server environments, the task to diagnose, troubleshoot, and resolve network and system problems includes remediating authorization bypasses in Docker [6], remote code execution flaws [8], and SD-WAN manager bugs [11], as well as patching messaging middleware [12]. The task to replace defective components is unlikely to change because current autonomous tools lack the physical embodiment required for hardware swaps [13].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, administrators broadly may shift toward oversight of autonomous IT operations and agent-state recovery, while subsegments integrate specialized agents for cloud and mobile security.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For administrators in these technology-integrated environments, if current trajectories hold, the task to diagnose, troubleshoot, and resolve network problems may shift toward the auditing of agent-generated diagnostics and the validation of autonomous fixes [10][2]. Extrapolating from predictive storage trends, the task to analyze network and server resource consumption could move toward continuous, autonomous capacity rightsizing [5]. The task to confer with network users about solutions to existing system problems is likely to persist unchanged because these interactions require organizational context and social nuance not present in technical logs [13]. High-level security policy definition within the task to plan, coordinate, and implement network security measures remains a human-led function due to the liability associated with infrastructure-wide access controls [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the administrator's role in these settings could shift further toward auditing AI-generated diagnostics and capacity optimizations.*

## Far (2046–2051)

Within these technology-driven environments, the evolution of the role depends on whether regulatory regimes grant autonomous agents the authority to execute structural changes in critical infrastructure. A primary unknown is the legal threshold for liability when an agent-led modification causes a catastrophic network outage. The task to design, configure, and test computer hardware and networking software resists full automation due to the high error cost of architectural failures [2]. The task to load computer tapes and disks—where physical media persist—remains a human requirement [13]. Rival outcomes depend on the intersection of liability law and agent reliability.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, administrators shift to a purely strategic role, defining constraints for fully autonomous infrastructure that manages its own lifecycle.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, strict liability mandates require a human-in-the-loop for every structural change, preserving the administrator's role as a mandatory manual validator of all system modifications.*

title: Computer Programmers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For this occupation broadly, the widespread adoption of agentic coding assistants and multimodal environments shifts the task of writing, analyzing, review, and rewriting programs from manual authorship toward the supervision of generated logic [4][7][12][13][14][15][16]. The mechanism for correcting errors is modified by cross-model review features that provide automated second opinions to verify logical consistency and reduce manual debugging time [5]. For a subset of workers in the logistics subsegment, specialized agents automate the task of writing and maintaining computer programs for high-complexity domains, such as shipping rate management [2]. For entry-level workers, the automation of boilerplate and basic logic reduces the demand for roles centered on routine authorship [3]. In the Android development subsegment, tools designed for robotic consumption rather than human readability shift the task of writing programs toward machine-to-machine communication [11]. The adoption of high-level prompting without rigorous verification complicates the task of conducting trial runs of programs, as "vibe coding" may lead to silent logical failures that evade superficial testing [8]. The task of consulting with managerial, engineering, and technical personnel to clarify program intent is unlikely to change, as agentic systems still require precise human specifications to prevent logical drift [5].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, computer programmers may transition from manual code authorship to the supervision of agentic generation, while the demand for entry-level roles focused on routine authorship may decline.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For this occupation broadly, if the availability of open-source agentic tools offsets the costs of proprietary systems [1], the revision, repair, or expansion of existing programs may shift toward iterative, self-correcting agent loops [5]. Extrapolating from the automation of routine scripts and cron jobs [9] and the integration of AI-driven development platforms for enterprises [6][12], the manual effort required to write and update programs for specific operational tasks may decrease. The task of compiling and writing documentation of program development is likely to persist as a human-led activity to ensure system auditability and regulatory compliance in high-stakes environments [5]. The task of investigating whether networks or peripheral equipment are responding to program instructions is unlikely to change, as symbolic agents lack the physical observability required for hardware-level troubleshooting [12].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may shift toward the validation and orchestration of AI-generated logic, with routine maintenance becoming increasingly automated across enterprise settings.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For this occupation broadly, the long-term trajectory depends on whether AI-generated code remains legible to human programmers. One plausible outcome is that the task of preparing detailed workflow charts and diagrams is replaced by the management of autonomous agents that handle the end-to-end lifecycle of maintaining computer programs [4][12]. A competing outcome is that the accumulation of opaque, AI-generated legacy code creates a complexity trap, where the loss of human mental models forces a return to manual revision and repair for systems that agents cannot safely modify without introducing regressions [3][8]. In classes of settings where workers train AI doubles to replicate professional workflows, as observed among tech workers in certain East Asian markets [10], the occupation may bifurcate between those who design agentic systems and those whose core tasks are subsumed by their own digital replicas. It remains unknown whether human programmers will retain the ability to audit code that was neither written nor reviewed by a human. The fundamental requirement for logical rigor in symbolic logic is unlikely to change, regardless of the authorship mechanism.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation may evolve into a high-level orchestration role where humans manage autonomous agent swarms that handle the entire software lifecycle.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a systemic loss of code legibility may force a return to manual, low-level programming to rescue critical systems from AI-generated complexity traps.*

title: Software Developers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For software developers broadly, the task of modify existing software is shifting toward the use of terminal-based agentic tools that autonomously write and deploy code within local environments [1][9][59][63]. The task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures is incorporating cross-model reviews to provide automated second opinions on code correctness [17] and the use of specialized models to identify and remediate vulnerabilities in large-scale legacy codebases [58][60][62]. For developers in XR and game development subsegments, the task of design, develop and modify software systems is moving toward "vibe coding"—the use of intent-based blocks [2] or single-prompt game generation [49]—which may increase codebase instability and technical debt [39]. For open-source maintainers tasked to supervise the work of programmers, the burden of vetting contributions is increasing due to the volume of AI-generated "slop" [13] and industrialized social engineering attacks targeting software supply chains [6][16][21]. This increases the criticality of the task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures, specifically regarding the manual verification of Git identities to prevent AI reviewers from accepting spoofed commits [46] and the patching of architectural vulnerabilities in communication protocols [53]. The task of analyze user needs and software requirements is unlikely to change significantly because agentic tools cannot independently reconcile design feasibility with volatile real-world time and cost constraints [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, routine implementation and deployment tasks shift toward agentic automation, while the cognitive load for maintainers increases due to the need for rigorous security vetting of AI-generated contributions.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For software developers broadly, if current trajectories in agent orchestration hold, the task of design, develop and modify software systems may shift from writing discrete lines of code to managing registries of specialized AI agents that execute complex workflows [29][32][37]. For those in security-critical subsegments, the task of develop or direct software system testing or validation procedures could integrate LLM-driven mutation testing to automate compliance checks and security auditing [3]. For developers in the digital health subsegment, the task of coordinate installation of software systems may shift toward managing distribution through centralized interoperability app stores [48]. In regions where professional workflows are being distilled into AI agents, such as in some Chinese tech sectors, the task of supervise and assign work to programmers may be partially subsumed by the management of "AI doubles" [50]. The task of determine system performance standards is unlikely to change because it remains anchored to physical hardware limitations, such as GPU communication bottlenecks [8][20], and organizational service-level agreements.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the developer's role shifts further toward the orchestration of autonomous agents, while specialized subsegments integrate automated compliance and distribution frameworks.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For software developers broadly, the future of the task of design, develop and modify software systems may diverge based on the resolution of current security instabilities. One plausible outcome involves the standardization of agentic governance frameworks that provide immutable audit trails for autonomous workflows at scale [26]. A competing outcome is that systemic risk from supply chain attacks [21] and the degradation of codebase integrity due to unvetted AI-generated code [13] lead to a regression toward highly restricted, human-only "air-gapped" development for critical infrastructure. It remains unknown whether AI-led remediation of vulnerabilities will eventually stabilize the software ecosystem or create a cycle of instability that collapses bug-bounty economies [25]. The task of confer with systems analysts and engineers to obtain information on project limitations is likely to resist full automation because it requires high-stakes negotiation of organizational constraints and human-centric risk tolerance.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the occupation stabilizes around the governance and auditing of autonomous agentic swarms within a standardized regulatory framework.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, systemic insecurity in the software supply chain forces a return to manual, human-verified development for all high-criticality systems.*

title: Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For software quality assurance analysts and testers broadly, the deployment of LLM-based vulnerability discovery tools, such as Anthropic's Mythos, may shift the task of identifying, analyzing, and documenting problems with program function toward the triage and validation of model-generated bug reports [9][16]. Simultaneously, the increase in low-quality, AI-generated code, referred to as "slop," may increase the manual effort required for identifying and documenting problems with program function, as analysts must filter noise from functional defects [3]. For a subset of workers in rapid-application-development environments, the rise of low-rigor "vibe coding" may increase the frequency of identifying program deviance from standards in submitted applications [6]. In organizations adopting LLM-based compliance tools, the automation of mutation testing may reduce the manual effort required to develop testing programs [1]. For workers in the autonomous vehicle subsegment, operational failures in urban and natural settings [2][8] necessitate more rigorous edge-case validation when designing test plans and scenarios [2][8]. In regulated industries using generative AI, the task of specifying standards for release readiness may shift toward formal verification using automated reasoning checks [12]. For workers testing agentic AI systems, the use of simulation frameworks may replace live API calls when installing and configuring recreations of software production environments [15]. The task of investigating customer problems referred by technical support is unlikely to change in this horizon because it requires interpreting unstructured, environment-specific user reports that lack standardized logs [17].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may diverge between a high-volume verification role focused on filtering AI-generated code and a specialized validation role focused on non-deterministic AI outputs and deep vulnerabilities.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For testers in high-complexity and safety-critical environments, if current trajectories hold, the task of monitoring program performance may shift toward managing dynamic updates informed by AI performance predictions [11]. Extrapolating from operational failures in autonomous deployments [2][8] and emerging ethics frameworks, the task of designing test plans in the autonomous subsegment may transition toward the orchestration of simulation-based edge-case libraries and fairness-audit protocols [5][8]. Because AI systems often fail "quietly" without obvious crashes [7], the core analyst role broadly may shift from identifying explicit bugs to detecting subtle drift and silent failures in non-deterministic systems [7]. Participating in product design reviews to provide input on functional requirements will likely persist unchanged because it depends on human negotiation of schedules and organizational priorities [17].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the analyst's role in high-complexity environments may transition toward the orchestration of automated simulations and the high-volume triage of AI-identified anomalies.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For workers in regulated and high-complexity settings, the viability of the occupation may depend on whether formal verification via automated reasoning can replace probabilistic testing for complex systems [12]. A primary uncertainty remains whether non-deterministic agentic software—where applications are generated from single prompts [13]—can be validated through predefined test plans or requires a shift to continuous, real-time behavioral monitoring. For workers in the autonomous subsegment, the task of designing test plans may be replaced by the management of synthetic environment generators. The requirement to validate that a software system meets a specific human-defined objective remains a point of resistance to full automation.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, testing in regulated environments may transition into a purely formal verification discipline, where the analyst manages mathematical proofs of correctness rather than executing test scripts.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the occupation may shift toward a continuous monitoring role, where the analyst manages real-time guardrails and behavioral telemetry for systems that are too fluid for traditional test plans.*

title: Web Developers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For web developers broadly, the deployment of terminal-integrated autonomous agents and general-purpose coding models may alter the task of writing supporting code by consolidating generation and deployment within the command-line interface [2][9][13]. Because cross-model review features are appearing in CLI tools, the task of evaluating code to ensure that it is properly structured may shift toward auditing automated "second opinions" produced by competing models [5]. For a subset of workers managing content-heavy sites, the adoption of AI-powered CMS platforms may shift the task of designing, building, or maintaining web sites toward managing automated structural deployments [3]. The task of incorporating technical considerations into web site design plans now requires optimizing site structure and metadata to ensure browser-integrated AI agents can accurately parse product data [4][12]. Furthermore, writing supporting code now includes integrating live AI browser agents directly into frontend frameworks [6]. While build speeds increase, the task of evaluating code to ensure it meets industry standards must now explicitly include verifying that automated tools have not neglected accessibility requirements [7]. For a subset of developers using specific cloud-based deployment platforms, context-aware AI may introduce new security failure modes in credential management, affecting how workers design and implement web site security measures [8]. For developers employing autonomous agent workflows, the task of evaluating code may shift toward remediating the technical debt generated by those agents [10]. Analyzing user needs to determine technical requirements is unlikely to change yet because this task requires interpersonal negotiation of ambiguous business goals and stakeholder constraints [14].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, web developers may increasingly rely on terminal-integrated agents for drafting and shift their focus toward auditing agent outputs, managing AI-native CMS deployments, and optimizing site structures for AI search and browser-agent discovery.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For web developers broadly, if the availability of low-cost or open-source autonomous agents scales to offset the costs of proprietary subscriptions [1], the task of selecting programming languages, design tools, or applications may shift toward agent-led optimization based on real-time environment constraints. Extrapolating from current cross-model review capabilities, the manual effort required to perform web site tests could decrease as agents autonomously cycle through planning, implementation, and verification [5]. For workers in the CMS subsegment, the continued adoption of AI-native platforms may further reduce the necessity for manual evaluation or recommendation of server hardware or software by abstracting infrastructure management [3]. The requirement to confer with management or development teams to prioritize needs persists because these tasks involve organizational politics and subjective value judgments that resist algorithmic resolution [14].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the occupation may transition toward the orchestration of autonomous agent pipelines for code generation and verification, provided the cost of deployment remains low.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For web developers broadly, the long-term trajectory depends on whether the structural model of web application databases and interactive interfaces remains stable [14]. One plausible outcome involves the high-degree automation of writing supporting code, shifting the developer's primary role toward high-level systems architecture and rigorous security auditing [9][13]. A rival outcome considers a fragmented ecosystem where manual oversight is mandated for critical security and accessibility compliance, maintaining a distinct manual "validator" layer within the workflow [7][8]. It remains unknown whether the browser-based interface itself will persist or be replaced by agent-to-agent communication protocols. The fundamental need for human-defined goal setting and the definition of business logic resists automation even at this horizon.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may evolve into a systems architect and security auditor, overseeing highly automated code generation pipelines.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may split into high-level designers and specialized human validators who ensure legal, accessibility, and security compliance that agents cannot guarantee.*

title: Web and Digital Interface Designers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For the occupation broadly, the acceleration of AI-driven site production may increase the necessity for manual auditing to incorporate technical considerations into Web site design plans, specifically to ensure adherence to accessibility standards [4]. Simultaneously, the rise of AI agents as primary intermediaries may reduce the relative importance of designing visual funnels to develop Web site maps and page templates [13] optimized for direct human browsing [2]. For a subset of workers in extended reality (XR) contexts, the integration of large language models with modular blocks may accelerate the ability to create Web models or prototypes [7] [1]. For designers in the media and publishing subsegment, the shift toward "zero-click" environments may pivot the task of developing Web site maps [13] toward the creation of niche community hubs and interactive entry points [7]. For designers of child-facing interfaces, new safety blueprints may introduce specific constraints when incorporating technical considerations [19] regarding age-appropriate safeguards [3]. In regions where regulatory mandates for AI content labeling are implemented, such as India, designers may need to develop new visual overlays to maintain continuous watermarks without compromising usability [8]. It is unlikely that the requirement to conduct user research to determine design requirements [4] will diminish, as human intent and behavioral propensity must be validated regardless of whether the interaction is agent-mediated [2][7].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation broadly may shift toward accessibility auditing and agent-readable architectures, while specific subsegments in XR, media, and child-safety experience accelerated prototyping and new regulatory or structural constraints.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the occupation broadly, if current trajectories toward agent-mediated commerce hold, the task of designing, building, or maintaining Web sites [8] may pivot from visual interface creation toward the design of structured data environments optimized for autonomous agent navigation [2]. This shift would prioritize machine-readability over aesthetic conversion funnels for standard B2C transactions. For a subset of designers using agentic platforms, the process of developing new visual design concepts [10] may shift toward the orchestration of conversation-based iterations and editable designs rather than manual layout adjustments [5]. However, the development and documentation of style guidelines for Web site content [9] will likely persist for high-value brand interactions where direct human sensory experience remains a competitive differentiator.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, interface design for a broad segment of e-commerce may shift toward agent-centric architectures, reducing the relative importance of visual layout optimization.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the occupation broadly, the long-term state depends on whether users fully delegate digital interactions to agents or whether a preference for sensory, visual browsing persists [2]. One plausible outcome involves the transition of the designer's role into an architect of non-visual interaction protocols for autonomous agents. A rival outcome suggests that accelerated spatial prototyping tools [1] could drive a resurgence in highly complex, immersive human interfaces as a premium alternative to agent-driven automation. A critical unknown remains the rate of hardware adoption for immersive interfaces relative to the speed of agent-based automation. Even at this horizon, the necessity of ensuring functionality against accessibility standards [19] is expected to persist because diverse human physical and cognitive needs remain a constant constraint on digital access.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role may evolve primarily into the design of machine-readable protocols for agent-to-agent commerce, rendering traditional visual interfaces obsolete for most utility tasks.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, a divergence may occur where utility tasks are agent-mediated, but a high-value niche of "sensory designers" emerges to create immersive, XR-driven human experiences.*

title: Video Game Designers
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of creators using agentic platforms, designers in small studios seeking publishers, and the broader occupation adopting volumetric AI: creators in prompt-based environments may automate the task of creating core game features, including storylines and role-play mechanics, by using agentic AI to generate initial implementations [4][5]. For the broader occupation, the adoption of photo-to-volume technology may reduce the manual labor required to prepare three-dimensional mock-ups [2]. In the subsegment of small studios, the use of specialized matchmaking platforms may alter how designers present new game design concepts to publishers to overcome discovery fatigue [3]. In specific organizational contexts, designers may utilize the creation of core game features and storylines within downloadable content to address corporate or legal disputes [1]. The task of balancing and adjusting gameplay experiences is unlikely to change yet, as it depends on subjective human "feel" and iterative playtesting that current generative tools cannot replicate [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, agentic tools may automate core feature drafting for a subset of creators, while the broader occupation utilizes AI to accelerate 3D prototyping.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For the same subsets of designers and organizational contexts: if agentic tools for prompt-to-game implementation become standardized, the task of devising missions, challenges, or puzzles may shift from manual construction to the iterative refinement of AI-generated outputs [4][5]. Extrapolating from the integration of volumetric AI, designers may further reduce the time spent on preparing two-dimensional concept layouts in favor of high-fidelity, AI-driven 3D prototyping [2]. The use of narrative DLC as a forum for corporate litigation is likely to remain a niche practice, limited by the commercial risk of incorporating legal disputes into consumer products [1]. Conducted regular design reviews likely persist unchanged because the evaluation of emotional resonance and player engagement requires human qualitative judgment [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, a subset of designers may transition from drafting to curating AI-generated missions and mechanics, while 3D prototyping largely replaces 2D conceptualization.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For the same subsets of designers: rival outcomes exist regarding the automation of creative logic, depending on whether agentic tools can eventually devise missions, challenges, or puzzles that maintain long-term psychological engagement [4]. It remains unknown if the capacity to turn photos into volumes will evolve to automate character biographies and role-play mechanics, or if these tasks remain human-driven to ensure narrative coherence [2][5]. One uncertainty is whether matchmaking platforms will evolve into fully automated curation systems that eliminate the need for designers to present concepts to human publishers [3]. The task of balancing gameplay to ensure commercial success resists change even at this horizon because it relies on the volatile and unpredictable nature of human player psychology [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, a subset of game design is reduced to the high-level orchestration and prompt-engineering of agentic systems for specific platform-based creators.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the prevalence of AI-generated content leads to a market premium on "human-authored" mechanics, preserving the manual creation of core game features to ensure commercial distinctiveness.*

title: Web Administrators
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For a subset of web administrators managing WordPress-based environments or content-heavy publishing sites, technical priorities are bifurcating between automation and defensive hardening. In organizations adopting AI-integrated CMS platforms, the use of sandboxed plugins and serverless scaling may reduce the need to manually implement updates, upgrades, and patches [1] or configure server hardware to manage traffic spikes [1]. Simultaneously, for administrators in publishing settings, the emergence of third-party AI scrapers [2] necessitates the implementation of specific web site security measures [8] and more frequent monitoring for unauthorized scraping patterns [1]. The use of passkey authentication alters the mechanism used to implement security measures [1]. Despite these shifts, the need to collaborate with development teams to resolve usability issues [9] is unlikely to change because usability requires qualitative human judgment of user experience.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, administrators within these subsegments will see a reduction in routine server maintenance tasks offset by an increased requirement to deploy technical countermeasures against AI-driven content scraping.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For these same subsegments of administrators, if current trajectories hold, the role may shift from operational execution to environment and access governance. Extrapolating from the move toward serverless architectures, the task of installing or configuring web server software [17] may become a negligible part of the workflow for those using AI-powered CMS tools [1]. If the AI content licensing market continues to grow [2], the task of implementing security measures [8] may shift toward managing granular, identity-based access and licensing rules [5]. Administrators may spend more time on these higher-level functions, which are governed by organizational policy rather than technical constraints. The core need to document application and web site changes [12] persists because audit trails remain a requirement for institutional accountability.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the technical administration of these environments will shift toward the governance of AI-managed configurations and the enforcement of content-access protocols.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For administrators in these specific subsets, the long-term trajectory depends on the resolution of the conflict between content publishers and AI aggregators. One outcome involves the adoption of standardized, automated licensing protocols that eliminate the need for manual blocking, shifting the role toward a purely policy-driven compliance function. A rival outcome is that adversarial AI scrapers evolve to create opaque, systemic server failures, increasing the demand for deep forensic skills to determine sources of web page or server problems [6]. It remains unknown whether decentralized web protocols will replace the centralized CMS model entirely. However, the necessity to test backup or recovery plans regularly [14] will likely resist automation due to the catastrophic cost of total data loss.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, the role for this subsegment may evolve into a compliance-focused function as content access and server environments become fully abstracted and automated.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, the role may shift toward high-complexity forensic troubleshooting to resolve systemic failures caused by sophisticated, autonomous AI-driven scraping and attack vectors.*

title: Geographic Information Systems Technologists and Technicians
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For GIS technologists operating in regions with national 3D city-modeling initiatives, such as Japan, the workflow for geospatial data acquisition is shifting from manual generation to the integration of open-access digital twins [1]. This shift reduces the reliance on manual digitizing of maps or keyboard entry of tabular data [2]. Instead, these workers primarily collect, compile, or integrate GIS data [2] by importing existing high-fidelity 3D models into local databases [1]. Because these open-access models provide a standardized baseline, the task of producing data layers [2] becomes an exercise in filtering and layering existing data rather than original creation. Technical support to users regarding the operation of GIS databases [2] remains unlikely to change significantly, as the complexity of software configuration and client-specific requirements still necessitates human mediation.

*Hypothesis: In the near term, for technologists in contexts adopting open-access city models, the role shifts from primary data creation toward the integration and management of standardized 3D geospatial datasets.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For technologists in these same urban-modeling contexts, if the adoption of open-access digital twins continues, the focus of maintaining or modifying existing GIS databases [2] may shift toward synchronization and version control [1]. The mechanism driving this is the transition from static map layers to dynamic models that require frequent updates to reflect physical urban changes. As the volume of open-access 3D data increases, the task of reviewing incoming data for currency and accuracy [2] will likely persist, as the reliability of government-provided models must be validated against local site-specific observations. The need to confer with users to troubleshoot applications [2] remains unchanged due to the inherent variability in how different organizations implement these 3D models.

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, for technologists in regions with mature digital twin infrastructures, the primary technical challenge shifts from data acquisition to the curation and validation of high-frequency model updates.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For technologists in regions utilizing these digital twins, the long-term trajectory depends on the resolution of the tension between open-access standards and proprietary urban data silos. If open-access models become the universal substrate, the task of designing integrated GIS spatial databases [2] may evolve into managing real-time data streams that automatically update the 3D environment. However, a rival outcome exists where proprietary constraints limit the utility of open models, forcing technologists to continue performing manual conversion of other sources of digital data [2] to bridge incompatible systems. It remains unknown whether real-time sensor integration will eventually eliminate the need for manual data review. Meeting with clients to discuss technical specifications [2] will likely resist change, as the conceptual goals of urban planning remain human-directed.

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, for technologists in open-data regions, the role evolves into the management of automated, real-time synchronization between physical cities and their digital twins.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, persistent data fragmentation forces technologists to remain specialized in the manual translation and conversion of incompatible proprietary spatial datasets.*

title: Document Management Specialists
content:
## Near (2026–2031)

For document management specialists broadly, the integration of AI-driven "intelligent layers" into storage platforms may alter how they implement electronic document processing, retrieval, and distribution systems [3]. Because these systems shift from static repositories to active intelligence layers, the task of identifying and classifying documents may move from manual metadata assignment to the oversight of automated, AI-driven classification [3]. Additionally, the adoption of digital annotation systems replaces paper markups with real-time collaborative layers, requiring specialists to modify how they administer document and system access rights and revision control to maintain the integrity of master documents [2]. For a subset of workers in manufacturing environments, the deployment of AI translation technology may alter the process of preparing and recording changes to official documents [1]. In these settings, automated translation allows for faster synchronization of compliance records across multilingual workforces, reducing manual overhead in managing regional document variants [1]. However, conducting needs assessments to identify document management requirements is unlikely to change in the near term because these tasks depend on specific physical and organizational constraints of the end user's environment [2].

*Hypothesis: In the near term, the occupation may shift toward managing automated classification and dynamic digital annotation workflows broadly, while manufacturing subsegments may partially automate the versioning of multilingual compliance documents.*

## Mid (2036–2041)

For document management specialists broadly, if current trajectories in intelligent file interaction hold, the task of implementing electronic document processing systems may shift toward managing self-organizing information ecosystems [3]. The mechanism driving this is the transition from manual indexing to systems where files function as an active layer of the organizational workflow [3]. For the subset of workers in manufacturing, extrapolating from current AI translation trends, the task of monitoring regulatory activity may shift toward the auditing of automated translation pipelines to ensure technical and legal nuance is preserved across jurisdictions [1]. Despite these shifts, documenting technical functions and specifications for content management systems will likely persist because underlying system architectures remain proprietary and require human-authored documentation for audit and recovery purposes [2].

*Hypothesis: In the mid term, the role may transition from managing static records toward the oversight of autonomous retrieval systems and the auditing of automated translation pipelines.*

## Far (2046–2051)

For document management specialists, the future of the role may diverge based on the evolution of digital provenance. One plausible outcome is that the development of document or content classification taxonomies becomes largely autonomous, shifting the specialist's role toward high-level policy governance of these autonomous systems. A rival outcome is that the rise of sophisticated AI-generated alterations necessitates a return to rigid, human-certified "gold standard" records, increasing the specialist's role as a legal custodian of authenticity. It remains unknown whether global standards for digital record-keeping will unify or fragment further across different regulatory regimes. The requirement to implement procedures for the secure destruction of electronic records will likely resist change due to the persistent nature of legal liability and statutory retention mandates [2].

*Hypothesis A: In the far term, specialists may shift primarily toward high-level system governance and the auditing of autonomous content lifecycles.*

*Hypothesis B (competing): In the far term, specialists may evolve into specialized authenticity certifiers, where the primary value is the legal validation of document provenance.*
